paras: The Red Star whitecap confrontation was an encounter on the night of January 27, 1903, in which two Black tenants, Dan Johnson and Link Hudson, fired on three whitecaps who came to their homes on the Peets place near Brookhaven, Mississippi. The visitors fled; the first report said one or more might have been wounded, while a later account from one of the Black men involved said the shots were fired into the air. The encounter came during a whitecap campaign against Black residents of Lincoln County that state and county officials prosecuted in the following months.

Johnson and Hudson lived on the place of Deloss (D. T.) Peets in the Red Star neighborhood, about twelve miles northwest of Brookhaven. According to the Port Gibson Reveille, Peets was a prominent merchant of Hazlehurst with large planting interests. Whitecaps had been active in the Red Star community that winter; Stewart Fairman, another Black resident of the Peets place, later testified that 50 to 75 armed men came to his home on the night of December 13 and warned him to leave.

The Brookhaven Leader reported that Johnson and Hudson had been warned before Christmas to leave their houses and that a second warning was served about a week before the shooting. Instead of leaving, the two men armed themselves with shotguns and waited for the whitecaps to return.

The Leader received word of the encounter just as it went to press on January 28. In its report, three whitecaps returned the night before and told the two men they had come to make good their threats, whereupon Johnson and Hudson opened fire at close range and the whitecaps retreated. The paper said it was believed one or more had been wounded but that no further particulars could be obtained.

A week later the Reveille printed a version attributed to one of the Black men involved. In that account three men drove up to the gate, and before they could make a demonstration the two men fired their guns in the air and the visitors fled. Johnson and Hudson did not recognize the men.

No report of a wounded whitecap, or of any arrest for the encounter, appears in the coverage. Within days, however, Ed Norton and John Falvey of the Red Star community were arrested on Fairman's affidavit charging them with threatening and intimidating him and other Black residents, and Russell Matthews was arrested on the same affidavit. At a preliminary hearing held at Governor Longino's request, Judge Powell credited the testimony of Fairman and Joe Currie and bound the three over under $2,000 bond each, and two of their alibi witnesses were charged as well.

In May fourteen members of the whitecap organization pleaded guilty and were fined $5 and costs and placed under $200 peace bonds. The court's leniency rested in part on the finding that the men had 'never actually committed any personal violence' but had ridden armed at night, posted notices and warned some Black residents to move. None of the court reports names Johnson or Hudson.

The encounter was reported only in Mississippi white papers, and no Black-press account of it was found. The Leader ran its stop-press item under the headlines 'Met a Warm Reception' and 'Whitecappers Fired Upon Last Night By Negroes,' hedging the details with 'it is said.' The Reveille's 'Tells of White Cap Experience' credited a Black participant as its source, and the Greene County Herald of Leakesville reprinted it word for word on February 6.

The Leader's editorials on the arrests the following week condemned whitecapping as 'nefarious and cowardly work' by 'men who ride around in the dark to frighten harmless negroes.' In June the New-York Tribune praised the Lincoln County prosecutions as 'A Lesson in Order,' attributing the notices to the jealousy of 'white trash' toward Black tenant farmers, without mentioning the shooting.

The two accounts differ on whether the shots were aimed and whether anyone was hit. The Leader's version was an unconfirmed report received at press time, while the Reveille's came later from one of the men involved and says the visitors fled before making any demonstration.

reader.title: Red Star whitecap confrontation
bases: A band of whitecaps served repeated night warnings on two Black tenants to leave their houses and returned to enforce them; the men stayed and were not driven out (A1, A3).

The Brookhaven Leader's hearsay report (A1) and the Reveille's account from one of the Black men involved (A3) independently agree on the warnings, the return of three men, the shots and the visitors' flight, though they differ on whether shots were aimed or fired in the air.
